angle: Founder's three sample courses dissected, plus 7 similar GitHub repos (fetched READMEs, Oct 2026)

sources.name: AI Engineering from Scratch (rohitg00)
sources.covers: 542 lessons, 20 phases: 0 Setup(13), 1 Math(22), 2 ML Fundamentals(21), 3 DL Core(13), 4 Computer Vision(28), 5 NLP(29), 6 Speech/Audio(17), 7 Transformers(16), 8 GenAI(15), 9 RL(12), 10 LLMs from Scratch(24), 11 LLM Engineering(17), 12 Multimodal(25), 13 Tools & Protocols(45), 14 Agent Engineering(54, ends with product-thinking lessons: frame task, assumptions, success metrics, feedback ratchet), 15 Autonomous Systems(22: METR horizons, AlphaEvolve, kill switches, HITL, RSP), 16 Multi-Agent & Swarms(25: A2A, consensus, MAST failure modes), 17 Infra & Production(29: GPU autoscaling, EAGLE-3, prefix cache, disaggregated prefill/decode, FinOps, chaos eng), 18 Ethics/Safety/Alignment(30: reward hacking, sleeper agents, jailbreaks, EchoLeak), 19 Capstones(87: 17 end-to-end + 9 deep-build tracks).
sources.structure: Each lesson = Learn or Build type, docs/en.md plus runnable code in Python/TS/Rust/Julia. Routine: read, build, run from repo root, keep evidence (command, exit code, output). Companion website aiengineeringfromscratch.com, AI tutor skill, 34 README translations.
sources.strengths: Enormous breadth; placement quiz (10 q find-your-level) and per-phase quiz (8 q); 3 staged projects with local graders (Retrieval Eval Lab, Agent Trace Debugger, Tool Call Firewall); some interactive explorables (gradient descent LR slider); capstone tracks; multi-language code; evidence-based progress habit.
sources.gaps: Too broad (math/CV/speech) for an interview-focused experienced engineer; no interview Q&A, no timed/mock practice; interactivity is thin and mostly outside the repo; no progress tracking or leaderboard; no difficulty/seniority tags; depth uneven; overwhelming length.

sources.name: AiEngg Cohort (aiengg.dev) - AI System Design by Gaurav Sen & Tanishq Singh
sources.covers: 6-week cohort: W1 Agentic system design (single/multi-agent, context engineering, memory, basic evals); W2 Search & retrieval (incremental indexing, ingestion, access control, guardrails); W3 Evals & agent security (datasets, LLM-judge vs human, regression, prompt injection, unauthorized tool use); W4 Deployment & CI/CD; W5 Observability, scaling, optimization (tracing, caching, rate limits, async, alerts); W6 Production capstone with architecture review and live presentation.
sources.structure: Marketing single page: each week = Theory bullets + Coding goal feeding one cumulative project; capstone showcase cards (Acuity, HandoffLint, ReconAI etc.) with design docs, repo, demo video; 12 live classes, mentor feedback, certificate; paid, WhatsApp chat.
sources.strengths: Clear job-shaped syllabus (system design + evals + security + ops); cumulative project; showcase of past capstones as social proof; mentors from big tech; frames AI engineering as system design.
sources.gaps: No public lesson content or sample lesson, no self-serve practice, no assessment or progress tracking, not free, cohort-gated and time-bound; shows what learners want (system-design framing) but delivers nothing reusable.

sources.name: AI System Design Guide (ombharatiya)
sources.covers: Chapters 00 Interview prep (147-question bank, answer frameworks + mock transcript, 10 whiteboard exercises, 2026 job market, FAQ), 01 Foundations, 02 Model landscape, 03 Training/adaptation (LoRA, DPO, distillation, RLVR/GRPO), 04 Inference optimization (KV cache, PagedAttention, vLLM), 05 Prompting/context (DSPy, injection), 06 Retrieval (chunking, vector DBs, rerank, GraphRAG, agentic RAG, ColBERT, contextual retrieval), 07 Agentic (MCP, A2A, multi-agent, computer use, durable execution), 08 Memory/state, 09 Frameworks (LangGraph, DSPy, LlamaIndex), 10 Document processing, 11 Infra/MLOps/FinOps, 12 Security (RBAC/ABAC, multi-tenant), 13 Reliability/safety, 14 Eval/observability (RAGAS, LangSmith), 15 Design patterns/anti-patterns, 16 Case studies (15 featured: real-time search, coding agent, multi-tenant SaaS, fraud detection, eval-gated CI/CD, MCP knowledge agent...), 17 Computer agents, 18 Voice agents, 19 Multimodal generation. Root: GLOSSARY, COURSES, TRANSITION_GUIDE (role transitions), RESEARCH-RADAR, PATTERNS.
sources.structure: Numbered folders of Markdown, Mermaid diagrams (flowchart, mindmap), comparison tables, reading paths between chapters, case study = problem + patterns + solution + diagram. Living book updated monthly.
sources.free_open_source: Free, MIT (4k stars); promotes paid 1:1 mock interviews
sources.strengths: Closest to interview intent: question bank, answer frameworks, whiteboard exercises, case studies, glossary, transition guide, research radar for freshness; 2026-current topics.
sources.gaps: Static markdown, zero interactivity, no code execution, no self-grading or spaced repetition, no tracking; no chapter template; case studies 01-05 unlisted; reference-style rather than teaching-style; not fun.

sources.name: AI Engineering Interview Questions (amitshekhariitbhu / Outcome School)
sources.covers: ~570 questions in 14 sections: LLM Fundamentals(~80), Prompt Eng(~30), RAG(~42), Agents(~54), Fine-tuning(~32), Vector DB/Embeddings(~26), AI System Design(~49), LLMOps(~53), Evaluation(~36), Safety/Ethics(~45), Multimodal(~35), AI Infra(~35), Coding/Practical(~32: attention, BPE, RAG, rate limiter from scratch), Behavioral(~22).
sources.structure: Single README of bullet questions; answers are external links (blog, YouTube) or missing.
sources.strengths: Good taxonomy of what gets asked, including coding and behavioral buckets; large question count.
sources.gaps: No actual answers on-page, duplicates, title-only entries, no difficulty or seniority tags, no classic ML basics, no quizzes, no solutions to coding tasks. Clear opening for in-site answers, depth levels, and practice.

sources.name: LLM Course (mlabonne)
sources.covers: Fundamentals (math, Python, NN, NLP); LLM Scientist (architecture, pretraining, post-training datasets, SFT, preference alignment DPO/GRPO/PPO, eval, quantization GGUF/GPTQ/AWQ, new trends: merging, multimodal, interpretability, test-time compute); LLM Engineer (running LLMs/structured output, vector storage, RAG, advanced RAG/DSPy, agents/MCP/A2A, inference optimization, deployment, securing LLMs). 23 Colab notebooks (fine-tuning with Unsloth/Axolotl/DPO/ORPO/QLoRA, quantization, MergeKit, AutoEval).
sources.structure: Roadmap-style README with topic bullets + curated external links + Colab notebooks and articles.
sources.strengths: Excellent roadmap split by role (Scientist vs Engineer); proves a roadmap graphic drives huge star counts; hands-on Colabs for tuning/quantization.
sources.gaps: Most sections only link out, no notebooks for RAG/agents/eval/deployment/security; no exercises, no assessment; doc inconsistencies.

sources.name: LLM Zoomcamp (DataTalksClub)
sources.covers: M1 Agentic RAG, M2 Vector search (minsearch, sqlitesearch, PGVector), M3 Orchestration (Kestra), Workshop data ingestion (dlt, DuckDB, marimo), M4 Evaluation, M5 Monitoring, M6 Best practices (hybrid search, reranking, LangChain), M7 End-to-end fitness assistant, Capstone RAG app.
sources.structure: ~10 weeks, pre-recorded lectures + homework + capstone. Live cohort adds deadlines, scored homework, leaderboard, peer review of 3 projects, certificate; self-paced has none. Bonus points for public sharing (LinkedIn/X/blog). ~$1-5 API cost, no GPU.
sources.free_open_source: Free; license not shown in fetched page
sources.strengths: Cohort mechanics with leaderboard, peer review and public-sharing bonuses drive completion and virality; capstone rubric (knowledge base, retrieval, eval, UI, monitoring); explicit cost transparency.
sources.gaps: Video-centric, thin written lessons, homework specifics hidden, narrow scope (RAG only), dates external.

sources.name: AI Agents for Beginners (Microsoft)
sources.covers: 18 lessons: intro/use cases, frameworks, design patterns, tool use, agentic RAG, trustworthy agents, planning, multi-agent, metacognition, production, protocols (MCP/A2A/NLWeb), context engineering, agentic memory, MS Agent Framework, computer-use agents, scalable deployment, local agents, securing agents.
sources.structure: Per-lesson folder: written README + short video + extra-learning links + Python code samples; ~55 language translations via auto-translate.
sources.strengths: Uniform lesson template (text + video + code + further reading); consistent small lesson size; huge translation reach.
sources.gaps: Vendor-tied (Microsoft Agent Framework/Foundry); beginner depth; no quizzes or exercises; no interview angle; videos missing for last lessons.

sources.name: AI Engineer Notebooks (calmrocks)
sources.covers: Sections 00-12, 34 Colab notebooks: Setup/cost hygiene, Model APIs (structured output, tool calling, streaming, caching), Evals I, RAG (hybrid, rerank, chunking, why RAG fails), Evals II (golden sets, LLM-judge, regression), Agents (loop from scratch, tool design, guardrails/budgets, MCP, Skills, harness), Adapting model (fine-tune vs RAG vs prompt, LoRA), Security (injection, OWASP LLM Top 10), Operations (observability, fallbacks, MLflow), Serving/inference napkin math, ML system design, Customer craft (scoping vague asks), Case studies (support assistant, contract extraction, red-team benchmark, deepfake detection) + capstone brief.
sources.structure: Colab notebooks with Open-in-Colab badge, framework-free raw API calls, one-line setup(), shared data/, every notebook ends with exercises; runs on free Groq API, no card.
sources.strengths: Best example of job-oriented, hands-on, zero-cost, exercise-terminated notebooks; evals taught twice; includes customer-scoping and napkin math skills; no-framework philosophy.
sources.gaps: Colab/Python only, no browser-native interaction, no auto-grading, GPU topics concept-only, no interview Q&A or system-design drills beyond one notebook, no Anthropic notebook.

sources.name: AI Interview Guide (guocong-bincai)
sources.covers: 28 modules (claims 20, ~670-727 questions): LLM basics, prompt eng, RAG, vector index optimization, agent basics, multi-agent, MCP & Skills, planning/reflection, agent observability, safety & evaluation, production deployment, frameworks, multimodal, inference optimization & frameworks, advanced RAG, AI coding tools, Python engineering, AI system design, Forward Deployed Engineer, test harness, resume & interview tips, interview question sources, project experience.
sources.structure: Questions per module with a recall illustration each; advice to prepare three versions of every answer (30-second conclusion, 3-minute with trade-offs, follow-up on verification/failure/alternatives); 7 role paths (LLM app eng, RAG eng, agent eng, training/inference eng, FDE, multimodal, safety/eval).
sources.strengths: Role-based tracks; three-depth answer framework is a great mechanic; covers resume, projects, FDE role, coding tools; illustration per question.
sources.gaps: Inconsistent counts, no visible Q text, static, no practice or grading, unclear sourcing and dating.

sources.name: Ai-Engineering-Roadmap (AgenticAiLabs)
sources.covers: OSSU-style stages with time estimates: Programming(4-6w), Math(6-8w), ML(6-8w), Deep Learning(4-6w), Specializations NLP/CV/RL(3-5w each), Modern AI: LLMs(2-3w), Agentic AI(2-3w), RAG(1-2w), Prompt Eng(1-2w), AI Tooling(1-2w), Capstones. Links DeepLearning.AI, fast.ai, CS231n, MIT OCW, HF course, OpenAI Cookbook.
sources.structure: Numbered folders of markdown linking out to free resources.
sources.strengths: Time estimates per stage; OSSU curated-path model.
sources.gaps: Link curation only, no original content, no assessment, outdated/mismatched links, heavy classical-ML emphasis.

takeaways: Gap in market: nobody combines interview-focused content (question bank + system design + coding) with real interactivity. Existing free assets are either static markdown Q lists (answers are links or missing) or broad from-scratch courses with no interview framing. Inferview's wedge is in-browser interactive practice with graded answers.

Use calmrocks' lesson template as base: each lesson ends with exercises, runs with zero cost (free-tier or in-browser/mocked LLM), and has a one-line setup. For Inferview, make these run in-browser (WASM/mocked model, simulators) so no keys are needed.

Adopt guocong-bincai's three-depth answer mechanic (30-second, 3-minute, follow-up with verification/failure/alternatives) for every question; add self-rating and reveal-on-click, which none of the repos offer.

Tag every item with difficulty, seniority level and role track (LLM app eng, RAG eng, agent eng, inference/infra eng, FDE, eval/safety eng, multimodal/voice). Existing question lists lack tags; role paths exist only in guocong-bincai.

Topic scope for experienced SWEs: skip heavy math/CV/speech; start at LLM internals and go to APIs, RAG, agents/MCP, evals, security, serving/inference economics, observability, FinOps, system-design case studies. Ombharatiya's 20-chapter map plus Phase 15-18 of rohitg00 define the frontier set.
Evals must be a first-class track (taught twice in calmrocks; weeks of aiengg.dev; rohitg00 projects). It is the most differentiating job skill, so give it interactive golden-set / LLM-judge labs.

Case-study system-design drills (15 in ombharatiya, 49 design prompts in amitshekhariitbhu) should be turned into interactive whiteboard canvases with rubric scoring and component trade-off sliders (latency/cost/quality), since only static diagrams exist today.

Retention mechanics copied from others: placement quiz + per-phase quizzes (rohitg00), leaderboard/peer review/public-sharing bonus (LLM Zoomcamp), cumulative project and showcase gallery (aiengg.dev), evidence-based completion (rohitg00). Add LeetCode-style streaks, daily question, spaced repetition and mock interview timers, which no source has.

Freshness is a retention driver: ombharatiya ships RESEARCH-RADAR, monthly updates, 2026 job-market notes; mlabonne's roadmap graphic got 85k stars. Plan a visible changelog/'what changed this month' and a shareable roadmap graphic.

Content hygiene lessons: avoid answers-as-external-links, inconsistent counts, dead or mismatched links, vendor lock-in (Microsoft), and unsupported claims; build link-check and count validation into CI, and a single lesson/question schema (like uniform lesson folders) for contributors.

Open-source model: MIT/Apache across nearly all; add CONTRIBUTING with a strict question/lesson schema so community can add items; avoid paid-upsell clutter (ombharatiya and Zoomcamp both embed paid add-ons), keep it free to build trust.

Add the 'forward deployed engineer' / customer-craft and resume/project-story tracks (guocong-bincai, calmrocks) and behavioral questions (amitshekhariitbhu); these are under-served and map to actual interview loops.

angle: Paid and MOOC AI engineering courses (2025-2026): what exists, how delivered, price, and the interview-prep gap

sources.name: Hugging Face LLM Course
sources.covers: Ch1 pipelines + Transformer architecture (encoder/decoder/enc-dec); Ch2-4 Transformers lib, Hub, fine-tuning, sharing; Ch5-8 Datasets, Tokenizers, classic NLP and LLM techniques; Ch9 demos (Gradio); Ch10-12 advanced fine-tuning, dataset curation, reasoning models.
sources.structure: 12 chapters, ~1 week / 6-8h each; text + runnable Colab notebooks (also SageMaker Studio Lab) + YouTube videos; no certificate yet.
sources.strengths: Free, ad-free, runnable in-browser notebooks, tied to the HF ecosystem, huge mindshare.
sources.gaps: HF-library centric; no system design, evals-in-production, cost/latency tradeoffs, or interview questions; no progress/skill assessment.
sources.free_open_source: Free; content open on GitHub (HF repos, Apache-2.0 style).

sources.name: Hugging Face Agents Course
sources.covers: Unit0 onboarding; Unit1 agent fundamentals (tools, thought-action-observation loop, messages, special tokens, chat templates); Unit2 frameworks (smolagents, LangGraph, LlamaIndex); Unit3 use cases; Unit4 final assignment; bonuses: function-calling fine-tune, observability/eval, agents in games.
sources.structure: Units with text + code; final assignment = build agent on a benchmark and submit to a student leaderboard; two certificate tiers (Fundamentals = Unit1; Completion = Unit1 + use case + final challenge); no deadline.
sources.strengths: Leaderboard + certificate gamification, framework-comparison approach, free.
sources.gaps: Framework-specific, shallow on production reliability, security, cost; no interview framing.

sources.name: Hugging Face smol-course
sources.covers: Instruction tuning (SFT, chat templates), evaluation (benchmarks + custom domain evals), preference alignment (DPO), vision-language models, RL, synthetic data, award ceremony/project showcase.
sources.structure: 7 units in units/ + notebooks/ folders; built on SmolLM3 and SmolVLM2; designed for modest local GPUs, no paid services; cohort-style release schedule with a final showcase.
sources.strengths: Post-training end to end on small models, cheap to run, community cadence.
sources.gaps: Training-side only; nothing on serving, RAG, agents, system design, or interviews.

sources.name: DeepLearning.AI short courses + Agentic AI + RAG course
sources.covers: Catalog: agents (crewAI multi-agent, Evaluating AI Agents, Long-Term Agentic Memory w/ LangGraph, DSPy, agentic KG construction, event-driven doc workflows), RAG (26h RAG course, multi-vector image retrieval, on-device memory), LLMs (Generative AI with LLMs 13h, Transformers in Practice 11h, Post-training of LLMs, GRPO RFT, Reasoning with o1, Llama 4), MCP and Computer Use with Anthropic, Claude Code, spec-driven development, Cerebras fast inference, Pydantic for LLM workflows. Andrew Ng 'Agentic AI' (9h55m): agentic workflows, Reflection, Tool Use, practical tips, highly autonomous agent patterns.
sources.structure: Short courses 1-3h: video lessons + in-browser Jupyter notebooks co-taught with vendor (Anthropic, Meta, OpenAI, LangChain, etc.); full courses 10-30h; Professional Certificates (Deep Learning Spec 127h, ML Spec 95h).
sources.strengths: Fast, bite-size, instant runnable notebooks, vendor-authored, always topical (new tech within weeks), Andrew Ng brand.
sources.gaps: Vendor-tool tutorials not transferable principles; shallow depth; no tradeoff/system design thinking, no assessments that resemble interviews; Pro membership $25-30/mo for graded assignments/certs (auditing free).
sources.free_open_source: Short courses free for now; Pro membership $25/mo annual or $30/mo monthly for assignments + certificates; not open source.

sources.name: Anthropic courses repo
sources.covers: Five courses: Anthropic API Fundamentals, Prompt Engineering Interactive Tutorial, Real World Prompting, Prompt Evaluations, Tool Use.
sources.structure: One folder per course with README + notebooks; recommended order; uses Claude 3 Haiku for cost; AWS and Vertex variants. Repo now archived/read-only.
sources.strengths: Very clean progression API -> prompting -> evals -> tool use; interactive exercise style with prompts you edit.
sources.gaps: Single-vendor, archived, no RAG/agents/serving/system design.

sources.name: Chip Huyen - AI Engineering (O'Reilly, Jan 2025)
sources.covers: 1 Intro/AI engineering stack/use cases/planning; 2 Foundation models (training data, modeling, post-training, sampling); 3 Evaluation methodology (LM metrics, exact eval, AI-as-judge, comparative ranking); 4 Evaluate AI systems (criteria, model selection, eval pipeline); 5 Prompt engineering + defensive prompting; 6 RAG, agents, memory; 7 Finetuning (when to, memory bottlenecks, PEFT); 8 Dataset engineering; 9 Inference optimization; 10 Architecture and user feedback.
sources.structure: 10 chapters ~500 pages; companion GitHub repo with ToC, resources, notes.
sources.strengths: The de facto canonical syllabus for AI engineering; strong on evals and systems tradeoffs; written for working engineers; widely recommended for interview prep.
sources.gaps: Book not interactive, no practice problems or code-along, no mock interviews; paid ($50-ish).

sources.name: LLM Engineer's Handbook (Iusztin and Labonne, Packt)
sources.covers: Builds an end-to-end 'LLM Twin': data ETL, feature pipelines, instruct/preference dataset generation, SFT then DPO of Llama 3.1 on SageMaker, evaluation, RAG with Qdrant + MongoDB, FastAPI inference service, AWS deploy, LLMOps CI/CD, monitoring (Comet, Opik), orchestrated with ZenML.
sources.structure: ~11+ chapters built around one running project; full code in repo.
sources.strengths: True end-to-end MLOps/LLMOps project, production stack choices explained.
sources.gaps: Heavy AWS/ZenML tooling lock-in; dense setup; no interactive learning or interview framing.

sources.covers: 12 chapters: intro to LMs, tokens and embeddings, looking inside transformer LLMs, text classification, clustering/topic modeling, prompt engineering, advanced generation tools, semantic search + RAG, multimodal LLMs, creating embedding models, fine-tuning BERT, fine-tuning generation models.
sources.structure: One Colab notebook per chapter (free T4 GPU); ~300 custom illustrations are the book's hallmark.
sources.strengths: Best-in-class visual explanations of internals; runnable notebooks; builds intuition.
sources.gaps: Model-centric; light on production, agents, evals, system design, interviews.

sources.structure: Live cohort: 33 live sessions across 11 lessons over ~8 weeks (3-5h/wk), 200+ page reader, 6 homeworks with solutions, 10+ h office hours, Discord, lifetime recording access; 4.7 rating from ~1,000 reviews.
sources.strengths: Practitioner-led, sells out, the evals topic is the hottest skill gap; community and office hours drive value.
sources.gaps: $4,200 price excludes most people; cohort scheduling; not general AI engineering coverage; no interview prep.

sources.covers: Systematically Improving RAG Applications (retrieval evals, synthetic data, fine-tuning embeddings, query routing); various 'AI engineer foundations', LLM apps, fine-tuning, agent cohorts.

sources.strengths: Direct access to practitioners, applied workflows, accountability from cohort.

Invited: Reza Shabani on training your own LLM, Harrison Chase on agents, Peter Welinder fireside.

sources.strengths: Code-first pedagogy beloved by software engineers; from-scratch implementations build durable intuition.

sources.covers: Example code and guides for common OpenAI API tasks: embeddings, RAG, function calling, evals, fine-tuning, agents, structured outputs; articles/ and examples/ folders, registry.yaml and authors.yaml feed cookbook.openai.com.

sources.covers: Linear/logistic regression, classification, numerical and categorical data, generalization/overfitting, neural networks, embeddings, intro to LLMs, production ML systems, AutoML, fairness.
sources.structure: Self-contained modules of animated videos, interactive visualizations and hands-on exercises, with check-your-understanding quizzes.
sources.strengths: Best-known example of interactive visualizations and inline quizzes in a free course; clear module granularity.
sources.gaps: Classical ML heavy, LLM coverage thin, no AI-engineering or interview content.

sources.name: Udemy / Coursera bestsellers ('The AI Engineer Course 2026' etc.)
sources.covers: Broad 35+h bootcamps: Python, LLM APIs, prompt engineering, LangChain/LlamaIndex RAG, agents, fine-tuning basics, deployment; reportedly 110k+ students on top titles.
sources.structure: Pre-recorded video, code-along, minimal assessment; constant sales ($10-15 typical, India ~Rs 429).
sources.strengths: Cheap, easy discovery, certificate-of-completion appeal, broad.
sources.gaps: Quality uneven, tool-tutorial heavy, quickly stale, no depth on tradeoffs or evals, no interview calibration, passive.
sources.free_open_source: Paid, low price (sale pricing from affiliate sources, unverified).

takeaways: Nobody owns 'AI engineering interview prep': every source teaches how to build; none offers practice problems with graded answers, mock interviews, or 'what would you say in the room' framing. That is Inferview's open lane.

Chip Huyen's 10-chapter outline (foundation models -> evals -> prompting -> RAG/agents/memory -> finetuning -> dataset engineering -> inference optimization -> architecture/feedback) is the de facto canonical syllabus; mirror its spine so the site feels authoritative, then add practice layers.

Evals is the hottest paid skill (Maven evals course $4,200, 4.7 stars, sells out). A free, interactive evals track (trace error analysis, LLM-as-judge validation, regression tests) would be a major draw.
DeepLearning.AI wins on bite-size (1-3h) lessons with runnable notebooks; use the 15-30 minute lesson unit and in-browser execution (WASM Python or simulated components) so no setup is needed.
Hugging Face Agents Course proves gamification works: leaderboard submission, two certificate tiers, no deadline. Replicate with streaks, tiers, and a public leaderboard for challenges.

Google ML Crash Course sets the bar for interactive visualizations plus inline quizzes; Hands-On LLMs sets the bar for illustrations (~300 figures). Combine: interactive tokenizer, attention, sampling-temperature, KV-cache, and RAG-pipeline widgets.
Anthropic's courses (API -> prompting -> evals -> tool use) show an effective progression and an editable-prompt exercise format; build in-page editable prompt/eval exercises.

Pain points of existing offers: vendor lock-in (AWS/ZenML, HF libs, OpenAI-only), staleness (FSDL 2023), high price (Maven $750-4,200), passive video (Udemy), and no sequenced path. Position as vendor-neutral, free, always updated via open-source PRs.
Cohort courses are valued for accountability and community, not content: add study groups, weekly challenge, Discord, and discussion on each problem to replicate the cohort effect for free.
Maven evals syllabus shows a high-value structure: 11 lessons, 6 homeworks with solutions, 200-page reader; mimic with lesson + homework + solution + reader-style deep dive per track.
Teach the build-from-scratch material as fast.ai does (top-down, code first) since the audience is experienced engineers; skip ML basics, add 'for software engineers' analogies.
Add a 'system design for AI' practice format (design RAG for 10M docs, cost/latency budget, eval plan) as that is where Huyen/LLM Engineer's Handbook content converts into interview answers.

takeaways: Question-type taxonomy to mirror in the product: (1) LLM fundamentals, (2) RAG, (3) agents/tool use/MCP, (4) evals, (5) LLM system design, (6) inference/serving infra, (7) practical coding with LLM APIs and AI assistants, (8) classic ML basics, (9) safety/guardrails, (10) behavioral/customer/product sense. Order tracks by JD frequency: RAG, prompting, LLM integration, agents, evals/observability.

Interview formats are new and distinct from LeetCode and should be first-class problem types: take-home (build Q&A over 50 docs + 20-question eval set, report recall@5 and faithfulness), debug-a-broken-agent (infinite loop), AI-collaborative coding (scored on prompt clarity, verification, decomposition, judgment), customer-discovery simulation, paper discussion, and trace/postmortem reviews.

Build graded, runnable exercises, not just Q&A: sandboxed Python/TS where users implement chunker, retrieval scorer, token-budget allocator, tool-use orchestrator, async retry/backoff client, rate limiter, in-memory KV store with transactions, eval harness, with hidden tests plus a mock LLM so no API keys are needed.

System design drills should follow the standard ML design rubric (requirements, capacity/token cost math, data flow, eval, hallucination mitigation, human fallback) with LLM-specific levers: caching/prefix caching, routing small vs large models, ~800ms latency budgets, spend caps per request, step-level tracing. Offer interactive calculators (token cost, KV-cache memory, GPU batching) and rubric-based self-scoring.

Company-tagged questions drive stickiness (as LeetCode does): tag with Anthropic, OpenAI, Sierra, Scale AI, xAI, Databricks, Perplexity, Google, Meta, Glean; include loop-structure pages per company showing AI-tool policy (OpenAI research/infra banned; Anthropic permitted and scored) and rounds. Label provenance and recency, since sources are anecdotal.

Existing banks (570-727 questions) are static bullet lists with external or no answers; the gap Inferview can own is inline detailed answers, difficulty, spaced repetition, quizzes, runnable code, progress tracking, and role-based paths (LLM app eng, RAG eng, Agent eng, inference eng, FDE, AI safety/eval) with a pre-interview crunch mode.

Evaluation is the differentiator topic: LLM-as-judge calibration against human labels and its biases (length, position, self-preference), recall@k/precision@k/MRR/NDCG, faithfulness, regression-testing prompt and model changes, CI eval gates, red-teaming, drift. JDs rarely list it (4.5%) yet interviews reward it; make it a flagship track.

Serving/infra content is a sizeable niche for OpenAI infra and Anthropic: single-GPU batching, continuous batching, KV-cache management, sampling API design, GPU scheduling, quantization trade-offs, training fault tolerance. Visual simulations (batch scheduler, KV-cache fill) fit the interactive goal.

Include behavioral and values content specific to AI labs: mission/safety alignment, RSP, 'time you were confident and wrong', handling confident-but-wrong model outputs in high-risk settings, ethics inside technical rounds, explaining limits to non-technical stakeholders. Provide a STAR story builder.

Do not drop fundamentals: Big Tech still runs LeetCode-style coding and ML basics (bias-variance, P/R/F1, gradient descent, attention from scratch at labs); include a compact ML refresher and 'implement attention/sampler/loss' exercises, but weight toward LLM systems (JD data: ~70% AI-first roles, 95.6% production focused, Python 82%, TypeScript 23%).

Offer both Python and TypeScript, plus practical stack coverage seen in JDs: FastAPI, Docker/K8s, CI/CD, AWS/GCP/Azure basics, vector DBs, Postgres, LangChain/LangGraph/LlamaIndex vs. building without frameworks (interviewers often ask for no-framework solutions), MCP.

Research caveat for planning: nearly all findings come from secondary blogs and aggregators; no first-person Reddit/Blind/HN threads, Hello Interview or interviewing.io content could be retrieved. Plan a community submission flow (anonymous loop reports with date, company, level, round format) as a growth loop and trust mechanism.

sources.name: LeetCode

Company-tagged questions tie practice to a real hiring outcome. Discuss turns users into a content engine. A free core with paid company data is a proven split.

sources.gaps: Closed. Beginner-to-intermediate STEM, not interview prep. Expensive to author because every lesson is custom interactive. Weak on open-ended or system-level design.

sources.name: Duolingo (mechanics)
sources.covers: Streaks, streak freeze (bought with earned in-app currency), leagues, streak-saver notifications, a Perfect Streak Week reward, and special streak app icons. Secondhand blogs only; no first-party data found.
sources.structure: One reported internal finding: users reaching a 10-day streak churned less, which prompted streak-saver pushes. The share of daily actives with a 7-day or longer streak reportedly rose almost 3x. Other figures (churn 28 percent, DAU up 36 percent, a streak wager lifting day-7 retention 14 percent) were unconfirmed and conflict between blogs.
sources.strengths: The streak is the best-supported habit lever. A forgiving streak (freeze, repair) reduces rage-quit after a miss. Small daily goal lowers the cost of starting.
sources.gaps: Correlation versus causation: the 10-day-streak finding may reflect selection bias. Leaderboard effect is unproven. Streak pressure can feel manipulative, and the numbers need server, push and email infrastructure that a static site lacks.

sources.gaps: Closed and paid for depth. System design only, with LLM and agent design shallow or absent. Practice is gated behind AI feedback that costs money.

sources.name: Advent of Code
sources.covers: Verified: a December advent calendar of small puzzles, solvable in any language. Puzzles unlock at midnight EST. Every puzzle has a solution under 15 seconds on ten-year-old hardware. Private leaderboards remain; the global leaderboard was removed after ten years. The FAQ asks users not to solve puzzles with AI. Sponsor funded. Copying puzzle text or building a lookalike site is disallowed.
sources.structure: One puzzle per day for about 25 days, a shared calendar moment, a subreddit for hints. Users can join late. Self-checking by examples.
sources.strengths: Scarcity and a shared date create a yearly return ritual and a social moment (people post and discuss daily). A finite calendar avoids burnout. Private leaderboards give community without toxicity.
sources.gaps: Seasonal only. No feedback beyond right or wrong. Text and inputs cannot be reused, so mimic the idea, never the content.

sources.name: Kaggle (progression and Learn)
sources.covers: Secondhand: five tiers (Novice, Contributor, Expert, Master, Grandmaster) earned separately in competitions, datasets, notebooks and discussions. Medals and community votes move you up. About 2,973 Masters and 612 Grandmasters out of roughly 23.29M accounts (2025 tally; older figure 530 Grandmasters). Learn micro-courses and certificates were not confirmed; the Learn page fetch showed only titles (Python, Data Viz, Pandas).
sources.structure: Per-category tiers with scarce top ranks, public profiles, medals from competition results and peer upvotes.
sources.strengths: Multiple tracks let different personalities earn status (code, writing, answering). Scarce top tiers are aspirational. Public profile doubles as a hiring signal.
sources.gaps: Needs a server, votes and moderation. Tiers based on peer upvotes can be gamed. Not a static-site fit beyond a simple badge model.

sources.name: Codecademy
sources.covers: Secondhand reviews only: free tier limited to lessons marked Free Course; Plus and Pro add projects, quizzes, full paths, a practice area and certificates. Streaks and lesson tracking reportedly work on free. Prices conflict across reviews.
sources.structure: Paths made of courses, with in-browser lessons, quizzes and portfolio projects.
sources.strengths: In-browser code with instant checking removes setup. Paths package courses into an outcome. Paywall sits on projects and certificates, not on learning.
sources.gaps: Gated projects frustrate learners. Beginner pace. Closed, and no interview focus.

sources.name: Anki and FSRS (spaced repetition)
sources.covers: Verified from Anki FAQ: FSRS needs fewer reviews than Anki's default algorithm for the same retention, and SuperMemo's newest algorithm is proprietary so Anki uses open options. The FSRS benchmark uses review histories of 10,000+ Anki users and the optimizer is open source. FSRS is described as an independent community project with open datasets (FSRS-Anki-20k, anki-revlogs-10k).
sources.structure: Cards are scheduled by a per-card memory model with a target retention setting. Vendor claim of about 25 percent fewer reviews is unverified. Independent forum reports on real-world gains are mixed, and no peer-reviewed trial of learner outcomes was found. The algorithm pages (The Algorithm, Benchmark) were not fetched, so parameters and license per implementation are unconfirmed.
sources.strengths: Spaced review runs entirely client-side with localStorage or IndexedDB, so it suits a static, free site. Gives a reason to come back on a schedule ('12 cards due'). Interview facts such as latency numbers and loss functions are ideal flashcard material.
sources.gaps: Only memorization, not skill building. Needs a good card set. Open FSRS implementations exist but verify license per library before bundling.

sources.name: Open-source education code (Khan Academy exercises, Exercism repos)
sources.covers: Secondhand search result: khan-exercises framework is MIT licensed, with exercises under a Creative Commons non-commercial share-alike license; the Perseus renderer was reportedly archived in 2018. Exercism tracks are reported as MIT or Creative Commons and the website as AGPL-3.0 (verified for the website).
sources.structure: General pattern across freeCodeCamp, Khan and Exercism: software under a permissive or copyleft license, content under a separate Creative Commons or copyright license.
sources.strengths: Establishes a safe model for Inferview: code under MIT or Apache, content under CC-BY-SA, both stated plainly. Shows contributors what they are agreeing to.
sources.gaps: Non-commercial clauses restrict reuse, so do not copy such content. Verify each LICENSE file before forking anything.

takeaways: Ranked retention mechanics for a free, static-first site: (1) a finite, ordered path with a visible 'next up' (NeetCode 75/150, LeetCode 75, roadmap.sh); (2) a daily ritual item shared by everyone, one new problem each day with an archive (LeetCode daily, Advent of Code); (3) a forgiving streak with a freeze or repair (Duolingo, the best-supported lever, with the caveat that its 10-day-streak finding is correlational); (4) spaced-repetition review of past material, run client-side ('N cards due'), which gives a scheduled reason to return (Anki/FSRS); (5) interactive, instant-feedback lessons with pretesting (Brilliant); (6) company/role-tagged tracks and a rubric tied to a real interview outcome (LeetCode company tags, Hello Interview rubric); (7) seasonal or contest events (LeetCode weekly contests, Advent of Code); (8) public profile with tiered badges (Kaggle, LeetCode monthly badges); (9) community discussion and contributed solutions (LeetCode Discuss, Exercism mentoring).

Fit for open-source, free, static-first: strong fit are finite paths, daily item with a date-derived puzzle, streak and freeze kept in localStorage, client-side FSRS review, in-browser interactive widgets, badges, shareable profile cards. Needs a backend, so defer or substitute: global leaderboards, live contests, mentoring, user-generated discuss, cross-device sync (use opt-in export/import, or a GitHub-issue or Giscus-backed discussion thread per problem).

Make the daily item deterministic from the date so there is no server, and archive it so latecomers can catch up. Advent of Code shows a shared calendar moment drives social chatter, and its removal of the global leaderboard shows private or friend leaderboards are healthier than a global one.

Build streaks forgivingly (freezes, weekend-safe goals, repair). Duolingo secondhand sources credit freezes with preventing burnout and streak-saver pushes with retention. A small daily goal, such as one question or one review batch, keeps the cost of starting low. Do not overstate causation in docs or copy.

Use a roadmap graph as the home page: nodes are topics, click opens a lesson, progress fills the node. roadmap.sh proves the repo format (one markdown file per node with a stable node ID) makes contribution a one-file pull request and scales to 371K stars. Copy the idea, not their content, which cannot be redistributed.

Teach with Brilliant's moves: pretest first (predict the answer before the explanation), manipulable visualizations (attention heatmaps, token budget sliders, KV-cache size calculators), instant feedback, mixed review of earlier lessons. Keep gamification light so content stays the star.

Mirror Hello Interview's four-layer ladder for each domain: core concepts, key technologies, patterns, worked question breakdowns, plus a delivery framework, an explicit interview rubric and a 'short on time' fast path. Their paywall sits on depth, so Inferview wins by keeping depth and practice free.

Pair every lesson with a practice problem whose answer is checked locally (multiple choice, ordering, numeric estimation, code in-browser) and a company or role tag (e.g. LLM app engineer, ML infra, applied scientist). LeetCode and NeetCode both put the company-tag data behind a paywall, which is the gap for a free site; rely on contributed, anonymized interview reports via pull request.

License as freeCodeCamp, Khan and Exercism do: code under a permissive license (MIT or Apache-2.0), content under a separate Creative Commons license (CC-BY-SA-4.0 or CC-BY). Their curriculum is under restrictive or non-commercial terms, so study the structure but never copy text. Avoid AGPL Rails stacks like Exercism's site; its maintainers do not support forks.

Content as files in the repo (freeCodeCamp curriculum/, roadmap.sh per-node markdown) with a typed frontmatter schema, a CI check, and a 'good first contribution' label gives the community a cheap on-ramp and keeps the site static. Add a contributor leaderboard or credits page, since Exercism and Kaggle show recognition keeps contributors.

Provide something tangible at the end: a verifiable completion record. freeCodeCamp's permanent, verifiable certificates, revocable for plagiarism, are a strong draw. For a static site, an unforgeable-looking but self-hosted shareable profile or readiness score card is feasible; real verification needs a signed backend, so label it self-reported.

Open question: the Duolingo, Codecademy, NeetCode price and Kaggle tier numbers all came from secondary sources and several pages returned only titles or 403. Re-verify before quoting any figure publicly.

angle: Best-in-class interactive and fun-to-read technical teaching for AI/LLM concepts: widget types, writing techniques, and what can run backend-free in the browser. Items marked (memory) could not be verified because the fetch returned an empty JS shell.

sources.name: Transformer Explainer (Georgia Tech Polo Club)
sources.covers: Whole GPT-2 transformer: embedding, multi-head self-attention, MLP, layer norm, dropout, residuals, output probabilities, sampling.
sources.structure: One page with a live model. Header has a prompt box plus temperature, top-k and top-p controls. Below are the architecture sections: What is a Transformer, Architecture, Auxiliary features, Interactive features.
sources.strengths: Runs real GPT-2 small (124M, from nanoGPT, via ONNX Runtime Web) in the browser with no backend. Users type their own text. Hover a token to see attention weights. Sliders show the distribution changing live. Built with Svelte and D3. Model and visualization are the same thing, so it is the best pattern to copy.
sources.gaps: Only one model and one architecture. Little on training, inference systems or interview-style questions.
sources.free_open_source: Free, open source (GitHub, Georgia Tech/Polo Club).

sources.name: Jay Alammar: The Illustrated Transformer
sources.covers: Transformer, self-attention, multi-head attention, positional encoding, residuals, decoder, softmax and loss.
sources.structure: 17 sections going from a black box to its components: high-level look, tensors, encoding, self-attention at high level, in detail, as matrices, many heads, positional encoding, residuals, decoder, final linear and softmax, training, loss.
sources.strengths: Progressive disclosure: one concept at a time, each built on the last. Running examples (the 'animal/street' sentence, 'je suis étudiant'). Toy dimensions (4-d embeddings, 6-word vocab) tied back to real sizes (512-d, 50k vocab). Box-and-colour tensor diagrams with labelled shapes. Animated GIFs. Candid first-person asides. Includes a Colab link.
sources.gaps: The page itself is static. No sliders and no way to try your own input.
sources.free_open_source: Free to read; the author's content is not under an open-source license.

sources.name: Jay Alammar: The Illustrated Word2vec
sources.covers: Embeddings, cosine similarity, word analogies, language modelling, skip-gram, negative sampling.
sources.structure: Hook, then a personality-vector analogy, word embeddings, language modelling, then the training mechanics (sliding window, skip-gram, negative sampling, hyperparameters), then a reading list. Dune epigraphs open sections.
sources.strengths: Starts with a human example: a Big Five personality score as a vector, compared with cosine similarity. Then king - man + woman ≈ queen using GloVe. Vectors are shown as red/white/blue heatmap strips, so readers compare patterns instead of digits. Uses rhetorical questions and 'fill in the blank' prompts. The sliding-window diagrams make training data generation concrete.
sources.gaps: Static. Word2vec is dated, though still good for teaching embeddings.
sources.free_open_source: Free to read; not open source.

sources.name: LLM Visualization (Brendan Bycroft)
sources.covers: 3D walkthrough of a small GPT (nano-GPT style): embeddings, layer norm, self-attention, MLP, softmax, output, with the actual matrix computations. (memory)
sources.structure: A fetch returned only a title because the page is JS-rendered. From memory: a guided scroll walkthrough, with a free 3D camera, over the real weights of a tiny model. Each block is a 3D tensor you can click and inspect.
sources.strengths: Shows real tensors with real shapes and real numbers. Guided narration anchored to the 3D scene. Comparison with larger models (GPT-2, GPT-3) conveys scale. Runs fully client-side.
sources.gaps: Not verified live here. It teaches the forward pass only. No exercises, no quizzes, and little on training or systems. The 3D view is heavy on mobile.
sources.free_open_source: Free; the repo is on GitHub (license not verified).

sources.name: Diffusion Explainer (Polo Club)
sources.covers: Stable Diffusion: text encoder, UNet denoising steps, guidance scale, seed. (memory)
sources.structure: The fetch returned only a title. From memory: an interactive overview with prompt presets, adjustable guidance scale and seed, and a timestep view that expands into the architecture detail.
sources.strengths: Same 'abstraction level' pattern as Transformer Explainer: the diagram expands into the underlying math. Presets avoid the blank-page problem.
sources.gaps: Not verified here. Image generation only, nothing about LLMs.

sources.name: Distill.pub: Why Momentum Really Works
sources.covers: Gradient descent, momentum, convergence, stochastic gradient noise, optimisation theory.
sources.structure: Hook that challenges the common intuition, a baseline, a closed-form model, applications, momentum dynamics, limits, extensions.
sources.strengths: Widgets with 'Step-size α' and 'Momentum β' controls beside the equations. Phase diagrams and convergence regions. Feedback handled through GitHub, with a citation block and BibTeX. Figures licensed CC-BY. Sets the bar for 'research-grade explorable'.
sources.gaps: Very costly to produce and the publication is mostly dormant. Math-heavy, with no interview framing.
sources.free_open_source: Free to read; CC-BY text and diagrams; code on GitHub.

sources.name: Bartosz Ciechanowski: explorable essays (e.g. Moon)
sources.covers: Non-AI topics (Moon, gears, lights), but the best model for the explorable style.
sources.structure: Long scroll essays with a small widget every few paragraphs. Each widget isolates a single variable.
sources.strengths: Draggable 3D scenes with camera lock. Sliders for mass, distance and eccentricity. Predicted trajectory drawn before release. Vector arrows and trails. Live plots. Scale-exaggeration toggles. Every figure is a custom canvas/WebGL piece.
sources.gaps: No AI content. The widgets are hand-built and very expensive to author.
sources.free_open_source: Free to read; not open source.

sources.name: Josh Comeau: Interactive Guide to Flexbox
sources.covers: CSS flexbox. Relevant for its pedagogy, not its topic.
sources.structure: Motivating demo, axes, alignment, sizing, gaps and wrapping, recap, bonus that unpacks the opening demo. Table of contents with anchor links.
sources.strengths: Live editable code playgrounds. Controls that toggle properties. A container-width slider to watch wrapping and overflow. Draggable kebab pieces as the metaphor. Asks the reader to predict an outcome before revealing it. Labelled callout boxes ('Way better on desktop!'). Self-deprecating first-person voice, pop-culture jokes, and a 'You made it!' payoff.
sources.gaps: CSS only. Course sales pitch at the end.
sources.free_open_source: Post is free to read; not open source.

sources.name: Nicky Case: Explorable Explanations (The Evolution of Trust)
sources.covers: Game theory through play. The fetch returned only a loading placeholder, so the details below are from memory.
sources.structure: Play a small game, then see the model, then tweak the rules, then learn the lesson. Short chapters with illustrated characters.
sources.strengths: The reader plays first, then reads. Cute, illustrated characters. Parameter tweaks for what-if exploration. Open licence and shareable.
sources.gaps: Not verified here. No AI content.

sources.name: Karpathy: Neural Networks: Zero to Hero
sources.covers: Eight lectures: micrograd (backprop), makemore bigram, MLP, activations/gradients/BatchNorm, backprop ninja, WaveNet, 'Let's build GPT', and the GPT tokenizer (BPE).
sources.structure: Video plus notebook per lecture, with exercises in the video descriptions. Only lecture 5 has a linked exercise Colab. Marked 'Ongoing'.
sources.strengths: Live coding from an empty file. You build up to a real GPT. Each step starts from the simplest thing and breaks it, then fixes it. Strong 'you could have invented this' feeling.
sources.gaps: Video-first and long. No in-page interactivity, no auto-checked exercises, no interview framing.

sources.name: Tiktokenizer
sources.covers: Live tokenization for models such as gpt-4o. Includes chat-message mode.
sources.structure: One screen: model dropdown, content box, 'Add message', token count, coloured token boxes, and a 'Show whitespace' toggle.
sources.strengths: Instant feedback while typing. Token IDs and coloured chunks. Surfaces surprises such as leading spaces, numbers, and non-English text. Chat-template mode reveals special tokens.
sources.gaps: It is a tool, not a lesson. No explanation of BPE, and no task like 'make this prompt cheaper'.

sources.name: Hamel Husain: Your AI Product Needs Evals
sources.covers: LLM evaluation: unit-test assertions, human and model review (LLM-as-judge), A/B testing, eval-driven iteration.
sources.structure: Motivation, the evaluate-debug-change loop, a Rechat 'Lucy' case study, three eval levels ordered by cost (L1 unit tests, L2 human and model review, L3 A/B), eval systems as a base for fine-tuning, and a conclusion.
sources.strengths: Anchored in one real product with real failure symptoms. A cost-based framework that decides how often each check runs. Concrete artifacts: a regex assertion, a synthetic test-generation prompt, a judge-alignment spreadsheet. Rules of thumb: read logs until nothing new shows up; prefer binary labels. Warning boxes (raw agreement is misleading on imbalanced data). Ends with a takeaway list.
sources.gaps: No interactive element. It defers RAG evaluation to another post. A course pitch at the end.
sources.free_open_source: Free to read; not open source.

sources.name: Eugene Yan: writing on LLM patterns and evals
sources.covers: Patterns for LLM systems (evals, RAG, finetuning, caching, guardrails, feedback); LLM-as-judge; prompting basics; lessons from a year of building. Also writing craft.
sources.structure: Practitioner essays with a clear problem-to-pattern framing ('How to Match LLM Patterns to Problems').
sources.strengths: Pattern-catalogue format that maps well onto interview and design questions. Pragmatic, opinionated, and honest about trade-offs.
sources.gaps: Text only. No exercises or widgets.
sources.free_open_source: Free to read; not open source.

sources.name: Lilian Weng's blog (Lil'Log)
sources.covers: Prompt Engineering, LLM Powered Agents, Adversarial Attacks, Hallucinations, Reward Hacking, Why We Think, Scaling Laws.
sources.structure: Survey-style posts with taxonomies, author-year citations, LaTeX, and figure captions.
sources.strengths: The most reliable single-page surveys. Taxonomy-first framing, for example scoping hallucination before discussing it. Good as a 'further reading' backbone.
sources.gaps: Dense and not fun. No interactivity and no exercises.
sources.free_open_source: Free to read; not open source.

sources.name: Sebastian Raschka: Ahead of AI magazine
sources.covers: LLM and ML research digests and from-scratch builds. The fetch returned only marketing copy, so no article list was verified.
sources.structure: Newsletter articles.
sources.strengths: Aimed at practitioners; educator tone per the testimonials. His from-scratch repos are a separate good reference (memory).
sources.gaps: Titles and structure not verified here.
sources.free_open_source: Free tier; the code repos are open source (memory).

sources.name: Browser inference stack: Transformers.js, WebLLM, Pyodide
sources.covers: Transformers.js: Hugging Face pipelines in JS for NLP, vision, audio and multimodal, with BERT, CLIP, Llama, Qwen, Gemma and Mistral variants. WebLLM (github.com/mlc-ai/web-llm): in-browser LLM chat. Pyodide (pyodide.org): CPython compiled to WebAssembly.
sources.structure: npm or CDN ES module for Transformers.js. WebLLM has an OpenAI-compatible API (CreateMLCEngine, chat.completions.create) with streaming, JSON mode, workers and several caches. Pyodide uses micropip, with NumPy, pandas, SciPy, scikit-learn and Matplotlib available.
sources.strengths: All three need no backend, so the site can be static and free to host. Transformers.js runs on WASM by default, with device 'webgpu' and dtype q4/q8/fp16 as options. WebLLM runs Llama 3, Phi 3, Gemma, Mistral 7B and Qwen2 at 0.5B to 7B. Pyodide enables 'edit and run this Python' for tokenizers, attention and sampling code.
sources.gaps: WebGPU is experimental in many browsers. First load downloads the model, which can be large (WebLLM warns the first load can be slow). Pyodide size and load time were not stated on the page. Not good for large models on phones.
sources.free_open_source: Transformers.js and WebLLM are Apache-2.0. Pyodide is open source on GitHub (license not confirmed from the page).

takeaways: Make the widget and the model the same object. Transformer Explainer runs real GPT-2 small (124M) in-browser via ONNX Runtime Web, and the sliders change the actual output. Inferview's attention, sampling and tokenizer widgets should use real tiny models, not mock-ups.

Use a fixed lesson skeleton: hook, intuition with a toy example, a widget that isolates one variable, the real-scale numbers, the code (editable), then an interview-style question. Alammar, Comeau and Distill all work this way.
Use toy numbers first, real numbers second (4-d embeddings, then 512-d). Always label tensor shapes on diagrams. Colour-code vectors as heatmaps so readers see patterns, not digits.

Use predict-then-reveal. Comeau asks 'take a moment to consider' before answering, and Nicky Case has you play first. Predict-then-reveal maps well onto interview practice and gives a reason to come back.

Offer progressive abstraction levels in one view. The overview expands into the exact math, as in Transformer Explainer and Diffusion Explainer. Beginners and experienced engineers can use the same page.

Voice: first-person, candid, a little self-deprecating, with one running metaphor per lesson, labelled callouts and a payoff line. Tutorials like Hamel's stay credible by anchoring on one real case study and giving rules of thumb, such as binary labels over granular scores.

Tool-like pages like Tiktokenizer work because there is no setup and feedback is instant. Ship small standalone playgrounds (tokenizer, context-window and cost calculator, sampling, KV-cache sizer) that people bookmark and return to.

A static site is feasible. Tokenizers, small-model inference (Transformers.js, WASM by default, WebGPU optional with dtype q4/q8), Python cells (Pyodide, with NumPy and scikit-learn) and WebLLM chat all run client-side. This keeps hosting free and lets contributors add content with Markdown and a widget component. Gate heavy downloads behind an explicit 'load model' button and cache it.

Plan for device limits. WebGPU is still experimental in many browsers, and first model loads are large. Provide pre-computed fallbacks (recorded attention maps, cached traces) so every widget still works without WebGPU and on phones.

Hand-built Ciechanowski-style explorables are too costly for hundreds of lessons. Build a small widget library (slider, step-through, token-strip, heatmap, matrix, live-code cell, quiz) and compose lessons from it.

Give every lesson a licensed, citable lineage. Distill's citation/BibTeX block, GitHub feedback and CC-BY figures build trust. Link to Alammar, Weng, Yan and Karpathy for depth instead of re-deriving, and use survey-style taxonomies (Weng) as the backbone of reference pages.

None of these sources has interview framing, auto-checked exercises, or progress and streaks. That gap is where Inferview's 'LeetCode of AI engineering' position is open: pair each explainer with a graded question, a code cell and a trade-off prompt.

sources.name: Fumadocs
sources.covers: React docs framework with layers: Core (headless search/content adapters), UI, Content Source (Fumadocs MDX official), CLI. Supports Next.js, Astro (with React), Waku, React Router, TanStack Start; static export, i18n, LLM integration, OG image generation, layout tabs, feedback.

sources.free_open_source: Free, open source (MIT per my knowledge, not verified on page)

sources.gaps: Docs-oriented, no built-in progress/exercise/quiz model; must build course/track/lesson UX yourself. Page did not detail search backends.

sources.name: Astro + Starlight
sources.covers: Astro-based docs theme; Markdown/MDX/Markdoc in src/content/docs/; site search and i18n guides. Astro islands: static HTML by default, hydrate components via client:load / client:idle / client:visible; React, Preact, Svelte, Vue, Solid can be mixed on one page.
sources.structure: Content collections in src/content/docs; islands for interactive widgets.
sources.strengths: Smallest JS payload (zero JS unless opted in), Pagefind search built in (from knowledge), client:visible lazy-hydrates heavy widgets, multi-framework.
sources.gaps: Docs-site orientation; app-like features (dashboards, auth-gated progress, heavy client state) are awkward vs a full React app; MDX+React islands share state poorly across islands (need nanostores).

sources.name: WebLLM (MLC)
sources.covers: In-browser LLM inference on WebGPU. OpenAI-compatible API, MLCEngine, streaming chat completion, web workers. Examples: Llama, Phi, Gemma, Mistral.
sources.structure: npm package; model records prebuilt; run in Web Worker.
sources.strengths: Real chat/streaming in the browser, no backend, great for 'watch tokens, sampling, KV cache' demos and a local AI-mock-interviewer.
sources.gaps: Requires WebGPU (not universal, mobile/Firefox/Safari spotty); docs page gave no model sizes. From knowledge: small quantized models (~0.5-4B) are roughly 300MB-2.5GB downloads, cached in browser; bad first-load UX. Must be strictly opt-in.

sources.name: transformers.js (Hugging Face)
sources.covers: Run HF models in browser via ONNX Runtime Web. Tasks: text classification, feature extraction (embeddings), QA, summarization, translation, text generation, token classification, ASR, TTS, image tasks. Backends: WASM (CPU, default) and WebGPU (device:'webgpu', flagged experimental). dtype: fp32, fp16, q8 (WASM default), q4.
sources.structure: pipeline(task, model, {device, dtype}) API.
sources.strengths: Small models (MiniLM embeddings ~25-90MB q8, from knowledge) make real in-browser embeddings/semantic-search/RAG-retrieval/tokenizer demos feasible on any browser via WASM; q4/q8 shrink downloads.
sources.gaps: Page excerpt gave no cache/size guidance; generation with large models is slow on WASM; WebGPU experimental.

sources.name: Pyodide
sources.covers: CPython in WASM. Bundled packages include numpy 2.4.6, pandas 3.0.2, scikit-learn 1.8.0, scipy 1.18.0, matplotlib 3.10.8. micropip loads pure-Python wheels from PyPI. PyTorch is NOT in the list.
sources.structure: Load runtime from CDN, loadPackage on demand; run in Web Worker.
sources.strengths: Zero-backend Python exercises with real numpy: implement attention, softmax, cosine similarity, BM25, tokenizer BPE, KV cache from scratch with hidden tests; judge in-browser (LeetCode-style).
sources.gaps: Runtime ~10MB+ first load (from knowledge); no torch, so PyTorch exercises need numpy-substitute or server; infinite-loop handling requires worker termination; no network sockets.

sources.name: Sandpack (CodeSandbox)
sources.covers: Component toolkit for live-running code editors with in-browser bundler; React examples; static and experimental bundler modes.
sources.structure: React components SandpackProvider/Preview/CodeEditor.
sources.free_open_source: Open source, Apache-2.0 (from knowledge); private packages are an Enterprise feature
sources.strengths: Easy embedded JS/TS/React playgrounds, file tabs, tests; good for TypeScript/JS AI-app exercises (tool-calling parsers, streaming UIs).
sources.gaps: JS/web only (not Python); bundler hosted at CodeSandbox by default unless self-hosted; docs page lists no limits.

sources.name: WebContainers (StackBlitz)
sources.covers: Node.js runtime in browser. Fully supported in Chromium desktop; Safari 16.4+ and Firefox only beta/alpha. Needs SharedArrayBuffer + cross-origin isolation (COOP/COEP); credentialless mode only in Chromium. Chrome with blocked 3rd-party cookies and Brave default can break it.
sources.structure: Boot VM, mount files, run npm.
sources.free_open_source: Proprietary runtime; commercial use needs a license (page links to /enterprise, terms not shown)
sources.strengths: Full Node + npm in browser for 'build a real agent/MCP server' labs.
sources.gaps: Licensing for a free public product is a risk, COOP/COEP constrains embedding and hosting headers, poor non-Chromium support. Not recommended for MVP.

sources.name: Pagefind
sources.covers: Static search library: indexes built HTML, ships chunked index; 10,000 pages searchable with <300kB total payload (typically ~100kB). JS API plus prebuilt UI; v1.5.0 adds Component UI (search modal, a11y).
sources.structure: Post-build CLI step over output HTML.
sources.strengths: Zero backend, tiny payload, works with any static framework, supports filters/metadata (track, difficulty) via data attributes (from knowledge).
sources.gaps: Only indexes built HTML (client-rendered content invisible); no semantic search (could be complemented by transformers.js embeddings later).

sources.name: roadmap.sh developer-roadmap repo
sources.covers: Content behind roadmap.sh. Per-roadmap folder roadmaps/<slug>/content/ with one Markdown file per node named <topic-slug>@<node-id>.md; scripts/ folder for sync tooling; pnpm workspaces, TypeScript, Prettier, GitHub Actions; shallow clone recommended; merged changes auto-sync to the site.
sources.structure: Roadmap graph (node ids) defined separately from per-topic markdown; contributions are add/edit topic files.
sources.free_open_source: Public repo with license file (type not shown; knowledge: content under restrictive/CC-style terms, check before copying)
sources.strengths: Node-id-to-file mapping makes contribution tiny and low-conflict; great model for an Inferview skill graph/roadmap where each node links to lessons.
sources.gaps: Site code is not in this repo's content model; content is short link-lists not deep lessons; no exercises.

sources.name: freeCodeCamp repo
sources.covers: Monorepo: api, client, curriculum, docker, e2e, packages, tools, .devcontainer, .husky; pnpm workspaces + Turborepo; React/Node/D3 topics. Contribution flow via contribute.freecodecamp.org, bug reports through forum then GitHub issue.
sources.structure: curriculum/ holds all learning content (format not shown on page; knowledge: challenge markdown files with frontmatter id/title/challengeType plus tests in-file); e2e tests; husky hooks.
sources.free_open_source: Software BSD-3-Clause; curriculum under /curriculum is 'copyright freeCodeCamp.org' (notably not freely reusable)
sources.strengths: Proven model: content-as-files with in-file tests, strong CI/e2e, devcontainer for easy onboarding, forum-first triage. Lesson: choose a clear content license from day one.
sources.gaps: Heavy infra (API, DB); not a template for a static site.

sources.name: Exercism website repo
sources.covers: Rails 7 + MySQL + MongoDB + Redis + AnyCable, Docker/LocalStack/OpenSearch, TypeScript front end.
sources.structure: Website repo is internal and public-for-reading only; README says no PRs accepted, local run unsupported, 'community-contributions-paused'. Tracks and exercises live in separate repos (knowledge: per-language track repos with config.json + exercise folders with .meta/config.json, test runners, representers/analyzers).
sources.strengths: Content separated from platform: per-track repos with config.json manifests and per-exercise metadata is a very scalable content-contribution model.
sources.gaps: Platform not forkable; AGPL and backend complexity are anti-goals for Inferview.

sources.name: NeetCode leetcode repo
sources.covers: Community solutions repo (~6.5k stars) with folders per language (c ... typescript), articles/, hints/, scripts updateCompletionTable.js, updateSiteData.js, verifySiteData.js, .problemSiteData.json, CONTRIBUTING.md.
sources.structure: Solutions by language; metadata JSON generated and verified by scripts in CI.
sources.free_open_source: MIT (repo). The NeetCode website itself is not shown to be open source.
sources.strengths: Pattern: generated site-data JSON + verify script in CI keeps community contributions consistent; completion table is a motivating contributor leaderboard.
sources.gaps: Only solutions, no platform code; NeetCode site is closed so no reference for the web app.

sources.name: Cloudflare Pages / GitHub Pages limits
sources.covers: CF Pages free: 20,000 files/site, 25 MiB per asset, 500 builds/month, 20 min build timeout; bandwidth not listed (knowledge: unmetered static). GitHub Pages: 1 GB site, 100 GB/month soft bandwidth, 10 min deploy timeout, 10 builds/hour soft limit, and not intended for commercial SaaS/business hosting.
sources.structure: Hosting comparison.
sources.strengths: Cloudflare Pages: generous, fast global CDN, custom headers file (needed for COOP/COEP if ever used), unlimited-ish bandwidth. GitHub Pages: simplest for OSS but 100 GB soft cap.
sources.gaps: CF 20k file cap constrains thousands of per-problem pages (mitigate by bundling data in JSON); large model files must not be self-hosted here (use HF CDN).

sources.name: js-tiktoken / tiktoken
sources.covers: WASM tiktoken (all OpenAI encoders, needs bundler WASM setup; lite build loads encoders individually) and js-tiktoken pure-JS port for envs without WASM. Alternative @huggingface/tokenizers (knowledge: pure-JS, loads tokenizer.json for Llama/GPT-style/BERT).
sources.structure: npm packages.
sources.strengths: Enables the signature 'tokenizer playground' lesson: type text, see BPE tokens, ids, cost, compare cl100k/o200k vs Llama.
sources.gaps: Page gave no bundle sizes; ranks files are large (cl100k ~1-2MB, from knowledge), so lazy-load on island visible; OpenAI-only vocabularies unless adding HF tokenizers.

takeaways: Recommended stack: Astro 5 + MDX + React islands (Starlight optional for docs chrome, but custom layouts likely better for a LeetCode-style catalog) deployed static to Cloudflare Pages. Reason: zero JS by default for fast reading, client:visible lazy-hydration for heavy widgets (Pyodide, tokenizer, WebLLM), multi-framework escape hatch, built-in content collections with Zod frontmatter validation. Runner-up: Fumadocs on Next.js static export if the team prefers all-React and wants app-like pages; risk there is heavier JS and Next coupling.

Use Astro content collections with a strict Zod schema: id, title, track, level, prerequisites, estMinutes, tags, companies, type (lesson|problem|quiz|system-design), license. Failing builds on bad frontmatter is the cheapest content lint.

Adopt the roadmap.sh node-id idea: a single skill-graph file (nodes + edges) defines the curriculum; each node maps to content files by stable id so renaming a title never breaks links or progress. Adopt the Exercism idea: per-track config.json manifests and clear per-exercise metadata so contributors add one folder and nothing else.

Adopt NeetCode's pattern: a CI script that generates site-data JSON (catalog, counts, completion tables) and verifies it, so contributions can be merged with confidence; add a contributor leaderboard/completion table to drive community.

Exercise runner: Pyodide in a Web Worker with numpy preinstalled (numpy/pandas/scikit-learn/scipy/matplotlib available, no torch) for 'implement attention / BPE / cosine search / BM25 / KV cache from scratch' problems with hidden unit tests; Monaco (or lighter CodeMirror 6, recommended for mobile and bundle size) as editor; kill worker on timeout. Use Sandpack only for JS/TS app-building exercises; skip WebContainers (proprietary commercial license, COOP/COEP headers, weak non-Chromium support).

In-browser AI is a delight feature, not a dependency: transformers.js (WASM, q8/q4 small embedding models) works on any browser for embedding/semantic-similarity/RAG-retrieval demos; WebLLM requires WebGPU and downloads hundreds of MB to GB (cache in browser), so gate behind an explicit 'Load model (~X MB)' button with capability detection and a pre-recorded fallback. Never host model weights yourself; pull from Hugging Face CDN.
Tokenizer playground: js-tiktoken (pure JS, no WASM bundler pain) for OpenAI encodings plus HF tokenizers for Llama-style; lazy-load ranks files only when the island becomes visible.

Progress without a backend: localStorage/IndexedDB keyed by node id, with export/import JSON file and a versioned schema; streaks computed client-side. Optional later: GitHub OAuth via Supabase Auth (free tier) to sync progress rows with Row Level Security; keep the app fully usable anonymously. Risk: localStorage is per-browser, so offer export and cloud sync early to avoid churn.

Search: Pagefind post-build (under ~300kB for 10k pages, ~100kB typical) with metadata filters by track/difficulty. Add optional semantic search later via transformers.js embeddings precomputed at build time.

Hosting: Cloudflare Pages (free, 500 builds/month, 20k files, 25MiB/asset, custom _headers) is the best default; mind the 20k-file cap by shipping problem catalog as JSON chunks. GitHub Pages is a viable fallback but its terms discourage commercial use and has a 100GB/month soft cap.

OSS governance: split licenses explicitly, code under MIT/Apache-2.0 and content under CC BY-SA 4.0 or CC BY-NC-SA (decide early); freeCodeCamp's curriculum being copyright-restricted and roadmap.sh's license caveats show ambiguity hurts contributors. Add devcontainer, husky pre-commit, CONTRIBUTING with a 10-minute 'add a quiz question' path, issue templates for 'wrong answer'/'outdated'.

CI pipeline: pnpm + Turborepo monorepo (apps/web, packages/runner, packages/content-schema, content/); GitHub Actions for typecheck, Zod frontmatter validation, lychee link-check, markdownlint/Vale prose lint, a headless test that every exercise's reference solution passes its tests in Pyodide (Node-hosted), Playwright smoke tests, and Pagefind index build; preview deploys per PR on Cloudflare Pages.

Main risks: (1) Pyodide cold-start (~10MB+) and no torch, mitigate with preload on idle and numpy-only design; (2) WebGPU fragmentation, mitigate with opt-in and fallbacks; (3) content staleness in a fast-moving field, mitigate with 'last verified' frontmatter date and badges plus CI flagging pages older than N months; (4) cross-island shared state, mitigate with nanostores; (5) COOP/COEP only if SharedArrayBuffer-dependent tools are added.
