sources.name: SWE-bench (princeton-nlp/SWE-bench)
sources.covers: Real GitHub issues paired with repo snapshots. The model must produce a patch. Variants: Full, Verified (500 human-confirmed tasks), Lite, Multimodal, Multilingual. (Verified by fetch.)
sources.structure: HF dataset with instance IDs like sympy__sympy-20590. Docker harness run via `swebench eval`. Needs about 120GB disk, so it is heavy to run locally. Cloud options: sb-cli, Modal.
sources.strengths: Real unit-test grading, so no LLM judge is needed. Good source for 'debug/patch this bug' practice problems. MIT license.
sources.gaps: Too heavy to run in a browser. Reuse needs hand-trimmed mini-tasks with pre-baked traces. One secondary source says Verified was deprecated for contamination (unverified), so check status before citing it.

sources.name: tau-bench / GAIA / AgentBench / WebArena / OSWorld / Terminal-Bench
sources.covers: Agent benchmark landscape (secondary, search results only). tau-bench (Sierra): tool-calling customer-service workflows, pass^k over 5 trials. GAIA: 3 difficulty levels, general assistant tasks. Also web, computer-use and terminal agents.
sources.structure: Each benchmark has its own repo and leaderboard. This URL is a blog overview.
sources.strengths: Interviewers at agent companies such as Sierra ask about these. Teach 'how do you evaluate an agent' (pass^k, trajectory vs outcome grading, contamination) with trimmed tasks and recorded trajectories as exercises.
sources.gaps: Blog sources are of uneven quality and some conflict. Verify each against the official repo before quoting numbers.

sources.name: Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard (BFCL), MTEB, RAGAS, BEIR
sources.covers: BFCL: tool-use evaluation. MTEB: embedding benchmark (56-58 datasets depending on version). RAGAS: reference-free RAG metrics (faithfulness, answer relevance, LLM judge). BEIR: retrieval. (Secondary; the URL is the RAGAS paper.)
sources.structure: Public benchmarks, leaderboards and pip libraries.
sources.strengths: Direct source of golden-set, retrieval-metric and judge-noise exercises: 'pick an embedding model', 'why do RAGAS scores shift with the judge'. All run offline on small samples.
sources.gaps: No practice problems exist. Inferview would need to build the exercises. Doc and repo URLs were not individually fetched.

sources.name: Hamel Husain and Shreya Shankar - AI Evals FAQ
sources.covers: 7 sections: fundamentals; error analysis and data collection; evaluation design (binary pass/fail over Likert, judge choice, trusting automated evals); human annotation; tools and infra; production (CI vs monitoring, guardrails vs evaluators); domain topics (RAG, coding agents, multi-turn, agentic workflows). (Verified by fetch.)
sources.structure: One long FAQ, about 154k characters, organised as questions with short answers.
sources.strengths: The FAQ is already phrased like interview questions, so it is a ready blueprint for the evals track and its question bank. It is also a free counterpart to the $4,200 Maven course.
sources.gaps: Text only, no interactivity. Cannot be copied; link out and write original content.

sources.name: Prompt Engineering Guide (dair-ai) and Anthropic prompt-eng-interactive-tutorial
sources.covers: dair-ai (verified): techniques (zero/few-shot, CoT, self-consistency, ToT, ReAct, RAG), applications (function calling, synthetic data), models, risks, papers, tools, notebooks, datasets. MIT, 79.6k stars, 13 languages (translations contributed via PRs). Anthropic tutorial (verified): 9 chapters (basic structure, clarity, roles, separating data, output formatting, step-by-step, examples, hallucinations, complex industry prompts) plus an appendix on chaining, tool use and search/retrieval.
sources.structure: dair-ai is a Next.js docs site with a Papers section and a Prompt Hub. Anthropic's tutorial gives a playground at the end of each lesson plus an answer-key spreadsheet.
sources.strengths: Proves demand and shows the translation model for global reach. The Anthropic exercise format is edit-the-prompt, run it, compare against the answer key.
sources.gaps: Neither has interview framing, graded scoring or progress tracking. The Anthropic tutorial depends on an API key and a paid model. dair-ai is largely a static reference.

sources.name: NVIDIA garak, promptfoo, Gandalf (Lakera) and LLM red-teaming CTFs
sources.covers: garak (verified): LLM vulnerability scanner, Apache-2.0, 9.7k stars, probe families such as promptinject, dan, encoding, gcg, leakreplay, packagehallucination, xss. promptfoo (verified): eval and red-team CLI, MIT, 26.5k stars, now part of OpenAI. Gandalf (secondary): 8-level password-extraction prompt-injection game, 279k attack dataset. Others: AI Goat, PortSwigger indirect-injection lab.
sources.structure: CLIs plus gamified CTF levels.
sources.strengths: Security and guardrails is an interview category (the earlier taxonomy lists safety/guardrails) with no interactive teaching in the other reports. A Gandalf-style game of attacking a mock model, with defences you layer yourself, fits the fun goal. Levels can run on a scripted or tiny model with no backend.
sources.gaps: No existing interview-oriented content. OWASP LLM Top 10 was not fetched. Can't ship live attacks against real models for free.

sources.name: Stas Bekman ml-engineering and AI-Infra-from-Zero-to-Hero
sources.covers: ml-engineering (verified): hardware (compute, storage, network), orchestration and SLURM, training, inference, debugging, GPU upgrade decisions, comparison tables. CC-BY-SA-4.0, 19.6k stars. AI-Infra-from-Zero-to-Hero (verified): curated MIT-licensed list of systems papers, split into llm_serving.md, inference.md and training.md, plus conference lists (OSDI, SOSP, MLSys).
sources.structure: Parts 1-7 of markdown chapters, and an awesome-list of links by topic.
sources.strengths: Authoritative infra depth for the inference/infra track and a source of paper reading lists. The CC-BY-SA licence means derived content must be share-alike.
sources.gaps: Written for infra practitioners, not interview prep, and static. Needs a layer of 'how to answer' content and simulators such as a batching scheduler or KV-cache sizer.

sources.name: vLLM / PagedAttention serving internals (paper, nano-vLLM, serving-internals lessons)
sources.covers: PagedAttention (KV cache in non-contiguous pages, like OS virtual memory), continuous batching, chunked prefill, gpu-memory-utilization tuning. nano-vLLM is a roughly 1,200-line Python and Triton reimplementation. (Secondary, search results only.)
sources.structure: Original paper, blog explainers, and a small reimplementation to read.
sources.strengths: The paper plus nano-vLLM is the best path to a 'toy scheduler' exercise that runs in-browser. This is the most likely serving interview topic and the one with the clearest visual demo.
sources.gaps: Throughput claims in blogs (2-4x, 3-10x) are workload-dependent and unverified. Content found was not interview-framed.

sources.name: Latent Space / AI Engineer World's Fair community
sources.covers: AI Engineer newsletter and podcast, Discord, weekly LLM Paper Club, the AI Engineer World's Fair conference, and meetups. A listing reports roughly 197k subscribers (secondary, unverified).
sources.structure: Newsletter, podcast, conference talks and a Discord-based paper club.
sources.strengths: The main hub where the target audience already lives. Useful as a distribution channel and as an editorial model (paper club = recurring habit). Talks and posts are good sources to link from lessons.
sources.gaps: No structured curriculum or practice. Hamel, Simon Willison and Eugene Yan's blogs were only asserted in the query and not fetched, so confirm before depending on them.

sources.name: Chinese-language LLM interview repos (LLM_Interview_Prepare, AI-Interview-Code, DeepLearing-Interview-Awesome-2024, CSDN write-ups)

AI-Interview-Code (about 557 stars) collects hand-written exercises such as self-attention and AUC, not LeetCode-style. LLM_Interview_Prepare (about 125 stars, last push Aug 2024) holds questions and interview write-ups. Posts report Agent/RAG/MCP questions becoming standardised, with a bank of about 200.

sources.strengths: Shows a big non-English demand and the 'hand-write attention/AUC' round, which the other reports flagged as an under-covered coding format. 面经-style experience reports are a proven user-contributed format.
sources.gaps: Mostly stale (a year or more) and low-star. Nothing India-specific was found, so India and other regions remain an open gap. No evidence of licences.

sources.name: anthropics claude-cookbooks
sources.covers: Recipes for capabilities (classification, RAG, summarization), tool use, multimodal, prompt caching, cost optimization, sub-agents, evals (tool_evaluation, agentic_search), observability, finetuning and third-party integrations. (Verified by fetch.)
sources.structure: Python notebooks in topic folders, with registry.yaml, authors.yaml, CONTRIBUTING and a lychee link-check config. MIT, about 53.8k stars.
sources.strengths: A concrete example of contributor tooling (registry, authors, link check) to copy. The cost_optimization and observability folders cover FinOps topics that interview content often skips.
sources.gaps: Vendor-specific, needs API keys, and has no practice grading. Anthropic's own prompt-eng tutorial URL was not fetched at the old repo name.

takeaways: Use public agent and eval benchmarks as problem templates: SWE-bench (patch a real issue), tau-bench (pass^k over 5 trials), BFCL (tool calls), MTEB and BEIR (retrieval), RAGAS (judge-based RAG metrics). Ship tiny local versions with recorded traces and unit-test grading instead of the full Docker harnesses (SWE-bench needs about 120GB).

Evals track blueprint: map Hamel and Shreya's FAQ sections (error analysis, binary labels over Likert, judge validation, CI vs production monitoring, guardrails vs evaluators, evaluating agents and multi-turn) onto Inferview lessons. It is already written as interview-style questions, and the paid equivalent costs $4,200.

Add a security and red-teaming track, which none of the six reports cover in depth. Build a Gandalf-style level game against a scripted mock model with layered defences, then a 'harden this system prompt' exercise, and tie it to garak probe families (promptinject, encoding, leakreplay, packagehallucination) and the idea of promptfoo-style regression tests in CI.

Make inference-serving the flagship interactive topic: a continuous-batching and PagedAttention simulator, a KV-cache memory calculator, and a toy scheduler exercise modelled on nano-vLLM (about 1,200 lines). Use the vLLM paper and stas00/ml-engineering as the reading backbone and AI-Infra-from-Zero-to-Hero as the paper index. Respect the CC-BY-SA terms of ml-engineering (share-alike).

Prompt engineering is table stakes and widely loved (dair-ai: 79.6k stars, 13 languages). Offer it as a short on-ramp module in Anthropic's tutorial format (lesson then playground then check) but use a mock or in-browser model so no key is needed. Do not make it the core, since the audience is experienced engineers.

Plan i18n and community translation from day one, since dair-ai supports 13 languages and the Chinese ecosystem has its own interview repos and 面经 (experience-report) culture. Chinese interview material stresses hand-writing self-attention and AUC and standardised Agent/RAG/MCP questions. Add a 'hand-write it' coding category. India-specific demand was not verified; do not claim it without more research.

Distribution: the audience lives in the Latent Space newsletter, Discord and Paper Club, and at AI Engineer World's Fair. Plan a weekly paper-of-the-week with an interview angle (a recurring habit plus shareable content) and aim launch posts at those communities. Treat the subscriber figures (about 197k) as unverified.

Build a research-paper reading list into the curriculum: each topic node links 2-3 canonical papers (vLLM, RAG, ReAct, SWE-bench and others) with 'what interviewers expect you to say about it'. Seed from the systems-paper index in AI-Infra-from-Zero-to-Hero. Link out rather than copy.

Copy contributor infrastructure from claude-cookbooks (registry.yaml, authors.yaml, lychee link-check, pre-commit, CONTRIBUTING) in addition to the schema ideas in the earlier reports. Add a cost-optimization and observability (FinOps) topic, which that repo covers and interview lists rarely do.

Licence hygiene when reusing ideas: dair-ai and promptfoo are MIT, garak and SWE-bench are Apache-2.0 and MIT respectively, ml-engineering is CC-BY-SA-4.0 (share-alike), and the Anthropic tutorial's licence was not found. Record each source's licence in a SOURCES file and write original content rather than reproducing text.

Evidence quality warning: much of this gap-fill rests on search-snippet blogs (benchmark landscape, Gandalf details, Chinese repos, Latent Space numbers). Items verified by direct fetch: dair-ai guide, Anthropic tutorial, stas00, AI-Infra repo, garak, promptfoo, SWE-bench, Hamel FAQ, claude-cookbooks. Re-verify the rest before publishing any claim.
